It can't hit closer than 3 tiles, and each shot hits ground or air, never both.
beware: Troops lined up behind a tank. The tank does not shield them, as fragments pass through.
Bowlers, Witches, Hog Riders and Balloons, which all suffer from the spray.

Spell Tower.role: Never attacks. Casts the defender's chosen spell: Rage, Poison, Invisibility or Earthquake.
use: Bait a Rage or Poison cast with a hero, Siege Machine or Skeleton Spell. Reloads are long, so a wasted cast buys time.
Do not expect one cheap troop to use up an Invisibility tower. Freeze or Overgrowth is the surer answer.
Freeze or Overgrowth it before it casts. Do not count on them to end a spell already running, so keep moving through Rage.
Destroy it before it casts and that spell is gone, as a destroyed tower casts nothing.

use.t: A Totem Spell does not bait it, so plan another way to draw the cast.

beware: Poison hurts swarms such as Witches and Bowlers.

beware.t: Earthquake takes a share of big ground troops' health. Air troops ignore it.

Super Wizard Tower.role: Merged tower. A bolt hits one troop, then chains to many others nearby, air and ground.
use: Keep support troops well away from your tank, so the chain misses them.
Freeze, Invisibility or Overgrowth stops the bolts. Save one for when your army walks into range.
A Totem Spell draws its fire away from your army.
beware: Clusters and swarms. Hog Riders, Balloons, Witches and Archers all suffer from the chain.
Big flyers still take a heavy first hit, so Dragons feel it too.

meet.t: A finished base has 2, made from 4 Wizard Towers.

Wizard Tower.role: Short range splash at air or ground.
use: Send a tank first, then kill it with Archers or other ranged troops behind.
Spread out in a line. Never walk a packed swarm into its splash.
Each blast hits ground or air, never both, so Balloons over a targeted Giant are safe.
beware: Clumps of small troops, ground or air, especially Balloons.

beware.t: Packs of Minions, which it clears quickly.

meet.t: A finished base has 2 Wizard Towers left, beside 2 Super Wizard Towers.

X-Bow.role: Rapid single-target fire with huge reach. Ground only at long range, or air and ground at shorter range.
use: Check the bow. Level means ground only, tilted up means air too.
A ground-only X-Bow cannot touch air troops, so send them at it.
Put a Golem in front and swarm it with cheap troops, or Freeze it.
beware: Slow, fragile troops in its long reach, as it locks on early and holds on.

Air Bomb.role: Hidden air trap that blasts everything flying in a small area.
use: Send one Minion or Balloon ahead on your path to set it off.
Spread small flyers out, so one blast cannot catch them all.
Expect them near a Town Hall, storage or Air Defense left outside the walls.
beware: Tight clumps of small flyers, which one blast can catch.

beware.t: Not Dragons. They and other tough flyers can mostly ignore it.
Lava Pups, if it goes off just as a Lava Hound dies.

Bomb.role: Small hidden ground trap that hits everything nearby. Air troops ignore it.
use: Lead with a Giant or other tank, which takes the blast with little harm.
Send one Barbarian ahead of Wall Breakers where walls meet.
beware: Wall Breakers at wall corners, where one blast can kill them.
Stacked Archers or Goblins, and any group standing still to hit a building.

Giant Bomb.role: Big hidden ground trap with a wide blast. Air troops ignore it.
use: Look for empty 2x2 gaps between defences, or a 4x2 gap for a pair of them.
Send one cheap troop through first, before you commit more around it.
Heal survivors straight away. Heroes and other big troops barely notice it.
beware: Groups of small and medium ground troops, and summons dropped before the area is clear.

beware.t: Hog Riders, as a pair of these can end the attack.

Giga Bomb.role: Always visible trap with a huge blast and strong knockback, hitting air and ground.
use: A few small troops can snipe buildings near it without setting it off.
Set it off early with one Yeti, which has 18 housing, before your main army comes.
Eternal Tome can take away the damage. Do not count on it, or on Freeze, to stop the push.
beware: Big packs walking through its zone. Its strong push scatters them off your planned path.
Do not count on spells to clear it. Plan on a real troop setting it off.

Seeking Air Mine.role: Hidden mine that chases one flyer and hits it very hard. Only a flyer of 5 housing or more sets it off.
use: Send a lone Balloon along your path first. Each mine it takes is one less for Dragons.
Minions are too small to set it off, so they can follow your tanks without losses.

use.t: Or lead with a Lava Hound, which can take the hit.

beware: Dragons, Balloons and Healers pushing on just after an Air Defense falls.

beware.t: Battle Blimps and a flying Grand Warden, which can lose most of their health at once.

Skeleton Trap.role: Hidden trap that releases Skeletons to distract your troops. It can be set for ground or air.
use: Bring splash. Valkyries, Wizards, Witches and Bowlers clear the Skeletons quickly.
Lightning clears a group near the Town Hall. A Golem's death damage does too.
Keep support behind Giants and Hog Riders, which ignore Skeletons hitting them.
Set to air, it ignores ground troops. Dragons can fight back, but Balloons cannot.
beware: Slow single-target troops such as P.E.K.K.A, which waste time on them.
Hero dives near the Town Hall that stop to fight.

Spring Trap.role: Hidden trap that throws the biggest troop it can reach off the map, or hurts it if too big.
use: Be wary of wall gaps and paths. Ground troops walk through them on to the trap.
Send one cheap troop through first. It only takes one troop, so those behind are safe.
That troop must arrive alone, or the trap picks the bigger unit beside it.

use.t: A Golem beside your Hog Riders takes the trap instead, so the Hogs stay in the fight.

beware: Mid-size ground troops such as Giants, Hog Riders and Valkyries, which can be removed for good.

beware.t: Golems and P.E.K.K.A lose health and time. Heroes and pets only take half damage.

Tornado Trap.role: Hidden trap whose vortex pulls your troops in and holds them, so defences and other traps can hit them.
use: Send a few cheap troops first, such as Barbarians or Minions, so it fires on them.
Miners and Battle Drills ignore the pull, though they still take its small damage.
Expect it near the Town Hall or core, beside Air Bombs or a Poison Spell Tower.
beware: Packs held under splash. Balloons pulled together are easy work for Air Bombs and Scattershots.
Small troops most of all. The pull is weakest on heroes and pets.

glossary.short: A path you clear so your main army walks into the base, not around it.
means: Troops head for the nearest building they want. If outer buildings are left standing on both sides, your army walks off along the edge and runs out of time.

A funnel fixes that. Destroy the buildings on either side of your entry point, and check both sides are clear before the main army goes in. What is left in front of the army is the way into the middle.

A poor funnel is one of the most common reasons an attack fails. Heroes, Baby Dragons, Wizards and Siege Machines are the usual funnel makers. At low Town Halls, a few Barbarians or Archers on each side do the job.
glossary.example: Send a small group down each side to clear the outer buildings, then drop your main army in the gap between them.

glossary.short: The middle of a base, where the Town Hall and strongest defences usually sit.
means: Most bases keep their most valuable buildings in the centre, wrapped in walls and other buildings. That centre is the core. The defensive core means the same thing, with the focus on the defences in it.
Getting your main damage into the core usually decides an attack. It is why guides tell you to save Rage or Freeze for that moment rather than spend them on the way in.
glossary.example: Rage your Valkyries as they enter the core, where buildings sit close enough for them to hit several at once.

glossary.short: A section of a base closed off by its own ring of walls.
means: Base builders split a base into walled sections. Each one is a compartment. Ground troops have to break in or get lifted over the walls, which costs them time.
It matters because you often want your army inside one particular compartment. That is why you aim Wall Breakers and Jump Spells at a chosen spot rather than at the nearest wall.
glossary.example: Cast a Jump Spell over the wall of the Town Hall compartment, so your Yetis walk straight in.

glossary.short: A tough unit sent first so defences shoot it rather than your damage troops.
means: A tank has lots of health and usually little damage. Its job is to reach the defences first and take the shots while weaker troops behind it do the real work.

Tanky just means hard to kill. Used as a verb, as in Lava Hounds tank for Balloons, it means taking the fire for someone else. A bruiser is a tough troop that also hits hard. A meat shield is another name for a tank.
glossary.example: Drop a Golem first. Once the defences are shooting it, send your Wizards behind it.

glossary.short: To make defences shoot one unit so the others get through.
means: Defences can only shoot so many things at once. Anything that draws their fire, or soaks it up, is protecting whatever you send next.
It does not have to be a big tank. Skeletons, a Totem or a Furnace can all waste a defence's shots for a few seconds, and that can be enough.
glossary.example: A Lava Hound sent in first soaks up the Air Defense fire, so your Balloons arrive unhurt.

glossary.short: When a defence picks a target and stays on it.
means: Most defences choose a target and keep shooting it until it dies or moves out of range. That is called locking on. A defence that has locked on to your tank ignores the troops walking past.

This is why order matters. Send the tank first so it gets the attention, then send the damage troops. It also tells you when to spend a spell, as Freeze is best cast the moment an Inferno Tower locks on to your key unit.
glossary.example: Let the Inferno Towers lock on to your Golem before you drop anything fragile.

glossary.short: The route your troops choose by themselves once you drop them.
means: You cannot steer troops directly. Each one walks to the nearest thing it wants to hit, then the next, and so on. Most take any building, but some have a favourite, such as defences, walls or heroes. The route that results is its pathing.

Good attacks are planned around it. You remove buildings or use spells so that the nearest target is always in the direction you want. Overgrowth and Invisibility can steer troops too, because they make buildings something your troops skip.
Air armies care about this as much as ground ones, since a flyer's route decides which defences it passes.
glossary.example: Clear the buildings on one side, and your pack heads for whatever is now nearest.

glossary.short: The main group of troops moving into a base together.
means: The push, or main push, is the group that does most of the work. A ground push is one on foot. Spells and supporting troops are planned around keeping it alive and moving.
A ground core in our tips means the same as a ground push, and has nothing to do with the middle of the base.
glossary.example: Place Healing Spells a little ahead of the main push, so it walks into them.

glossary.short: The unit your attack relies on for most of its damage.
means: Borrowed from other games. The carry is what actually destroys the base, while tanks and support keep it alive. A damage carry and a main carry are the same idea.
Saying a troop cannot carry an attack means it is too weak to win without something else doing the heavy lifting.
glossary.example: In a Root Rider Yeti attack, Super Yetis carry the core once Root Riders have opened the way.

glossary.short: A heavy ground attack that breaks through a base by force.
means: A smash sends a tough, hard hitting ground group through walls and defences together, with a tank in front. It relies on raw power more than on precise spell placement. Yetis, Super Yetis and Root Riders are the usual smash troops.
It works best once a funnel lets the group go in as one, and it suffers against splash damage because the troops stay bunched. The Monolith also hits its high health troops hard.
glossary.example: A Yeti and Super Wizard Smash opens one side with heroes and a Log Launcher, then pours everything through the gap.

glossary.short: Dropping a lot of one troop in a wide line and letting numbers do the work.
means: Spam means less careful placement and more troops. You spread them across a wide front so no single defence can deal with all of them.
It is usually easier to do than a planned attack, but it gives you less control. Our guide contrasts it with controlled ground movement.
glossary.example: Yeti Super Archer Spam: drop a wide line of Yetis, then Super Archers behind them.

glossary.short: An army built almost entirely from one troop.
means: Mass Dragons means nearly all your housing space goes on Dragons. Mass Witches and Mass Hog Riders work the same way.
These armies are often the easiest to learn, because every troop does the same job. They can also be stopped by one thing that beats that troop, such as enough Air Defenses against Dragons.
glossary.example: Mass Dragons is the classic beginner army at TH7.

glossary.short: A hero sent through a base early, kept alive by support, to clear the way.
means: In a hero walk, one hero spends a long time moving through the base at the start of the attack, removing buildings and defences. Healers, Invisibility or other spells keep them alive. The main army comes afterwards through the space they cleared.

Players use walk and charge in two ways. Some say a walk stays near the edge to shape a funnel, and a charge goes deep. Others treat them as the same technique, with a charge just being the bigger job. Expect guides to mix them up, as ours sometimes does.
glossary.example: Walk the Royal Champion with Invisibility down one side, then send Dragons along the path she opened.

glossary.short: A hero sent deep to remove key defences before the main army follows.
means: A charge asks more of the hero than a walk. The hero goes further in and takes out defences that matter, such as an Inferno Tower or Spell Tower, with more spells and support to match.

The army that follows is a separate job. A good charge can still fail if the follow-up is mistimed, and a weak charge leaves that army facing a full base. The word is used loosely, so a walk in one guide may be a charge in another.
glossary.example: Charge the Dragon Duke along one side using Invisibility, then send your air army.

glossary.short: Sending a hero or small group straight into the dangerous part of a base.
means: Diving means going in deep, often alone, to hit something important. It skips the slow work of clearing a route, and the unit is exposed once it gets there.
It only pays off if what it destroys is worth what you might lose. That is why diving heroes often bring a Phoenix or a Spirit Fox, or have a Druid alongside them.
glossary.example: The Royal Champion dives over walls and goes for defences, so staying alive decides how far she gets.

glossary.short: Usually a Queen Charge followed by Hog Riders and Miners.
means: The name comes from mixing two ways of winning. The Queen carves out one side. Send Hog Riders and Miners only once she has removed the splash defences on their path, or the swarm melts.
Hybrid can also just mean a mix of two troop types. When our guide says air and hybrid attacks, it means armies that mix air and ground.
glossary.example: Queen Charge Hybrid: the Queen clears one side, then Hog Riders and Miners go in together.

glossary.short: The troops or spells that finish off whatever your main army left behind.
means: Your main army often destroys the core and leaves small buildings around the edge. Those still count towards your percentage and the last star, so something has to reach them before time runs out.
Cheap, fast troops suit this well. Keep a few back rather than dropping them all at the start.
glossary.example: Spread your last Archers around the base to clean up what the Giants did not reach.

glossary.short: Pulling the enemy's Clan Castle troops out so you can kill them away from your army.
means: Enemy Clan Castle troops stay inside until an attacker comes close. A lure is a small troop sent near the castle to bring them out early.
It matters because those troops can wreck a hero or a push that meets them by surprise. Once they are out, you can kill them with a Poison Spell, Lightning, or your own troops.
glossary.example: Drop one Barbarian so it walks into the Clan Castle range, then kill the troops that come out before your main army arrives.

glossary.short: To take out one chosen target from a distance, or with little effort.
means: Most often it means killing one chosen building, usually a defence, without fighting through everything around it. It can be done with long range troops, hero equipment or spells. Our guide uses it for removing an Air Defense with Lightning.
Players also use it for a quick cheap attack that grabs one star, such as going straight for an exposed Town Hall.
glossary.example: Snipe an Air Defense with Lightning Spells before your Dragons deploy.

glossary.short: When troops get held up, wasting time and taking damage.
means: A troop stalls when it stops making progress, usually because it is chewing through walls or stuck on buildings that do not matter. While it does that, the defences keep shooting it and the clock keeps running.
It is the problem Wall Breakers, Jump Spells and Overgrowth exist to solve, and often the moment to use a Rage Spell.
glossary.example: Valkyries stall at a wall they cannot get past, so have an entry ready before you send them.

glossary.short: A cheap unit or spell that wastes a defence's attention.
means: A distraction exists to be shot at. It buys your important troops a few seconds or sends a defence in the wrong direction. Unlike a tank, it does not need much health, only good timing.
It works best against single target defences, which can only deal with one thing at a time.
glossary.example: A Skeleton Spell on the Monolith gives it something worthless to shoot.

glossary.short: One side of the base, as seen from where you attack.
means: Attacks are often planned side by side. You might clear the left flank with one hero and the right with another, leaving a clean way into the middle.
A two-flank attack hits two sides at once, so defences have to split their fire. Our guide also says side or shoulders for the same thing.
glossary.example: Drop a Siege Barracks on one flank and a hero on the other to make a funnel.

glossary.short: The ring between a base's outer buildings and its core.
means: Your troops have got past the outside, but have not reached the centre yet. This is often where Air Defenses and other strong defences start reaching them, and where an army can slow down.
Guides mention it when timing a spell, so that it lands as troops enter this part of the base rather than too early or too late.
glossary.example: Cast Haste on Balloons as they push past mid-base, so they do not stall under Air Defenses.

glossary.short: When the attack clock reaches zero before you have finished the base.
means: An attack lasts three minutes once it starts. When the clock reaches zero the attack stops, and you keep only what you have already earned. A time out can cost you the last star even when the army is still alive.
Slow troops are most at risk. So is any plan that spends too long clearing the outside, or a long hero walk that uses up the time your main army needs.
glossary.example: Electro Dragons are very slow, so a long route can run out the clock with buildings still standing.

glossary.short: Flying a Battle Blimp over the base to drop your Clan Castle troops on a target.
means: A Battle Blimp is a Siege Machine that flies towards the Town Hall. It releases your Clan Castle troops when it arrives or is destroyed, or when you self-destruct it, so you can choose where they land. Used on purpose, it lands strong troops deep in the base early on, where they take out a key defence.

Super Archers are a common load, often with Invisibility or Clone Spells where they land. It is delicate, as Air Defenses and Seeking Air Mines can bring the Blimp down early. A Lava Hound sent alongside it can take the Air Defense fire.
glossary.example: Fly Super Archers in on a Battle Blimp, then cast Invisibility and Clone where they drop.
Hold the Royal Champion back, then drop her to finish the back end defences.
glossary.short: The far side of the base from where you went in.
means: An attack starts on one side and works across. The back end is whatever is left on the far side once the main army has been through.
It is where attacks run out of steam, so it often decides the last star. Guides save a hero, a Freeze or clean-up troops for it.

glossary.example: Fire the Warden's Fireball at stacked defences, so one blast opens a whole section of the base.
glossary.short: Built or bunched close together, so one hit catches several.
means: Stacked defences sit side by side, so one Fireball or Earthquake can hit several at once. That makes them a good target.
It works against you too. Stacked troops can all go down to one Mortar shell or bomb, which is why guides tell you to spread them.

glossary.example: Drop Bat Spells once the Wizard Towers are down, as one splash shot can kill a whole group of Bats.
glossary.short: A lot of small troops at once, so a defence cannot kill them fast enough.
means: A swarm beats defences that hit one target at a time, as each shot only kills one small troop. It also wastes the time of a single-target Inferno Tower.
Splash and multi-target defences are what beat it, so clear those first or keep the swarm spread out.

glossary.example: Bait the Spell Tower with a Skeleton Spell, so it is reloading when your main army arrives.
glossary.short: Something sent to set off a defence, trap or Spell Tower early.
means: A cheap unit goes first, so the danger goes off on it and not on your main troops. A bomb, a hidden trap or a Spell Tower's cast can all be wasted this way.
It differs from a distraction. A distraction keeps a defence busy, while bait uses up something that fires once or has a long reload.

glossary.example: Against a ring base, pick one place to break in, then keep your main army together through that gap.
glossary.short: A base with its core inside a ring of walls or buildings, often around a central Town Hall.
means: Getting through the ring is the hard part. An army with no way in can walk around it and run out of time, so plan your entry when you scout.

glossary.short: Killing a defence outright with spells, usually Lightning and Earthquake, before the army goes in.
means: To zap a defence, you hit it with enough Lightning Spells to destroy it, often adding an Earthquake Spell to save a Lightning. In an army name, it tells you what is being removed so the main troops have an easy run.

Zap Dragons clears Air Defenses and Zap Witches clears Inferno Towers. Zap Lalo hits an Air Defense or the defending Queen, whichever threatens the Balloons most. Work out how many spells it takes first, as a defence left on a sliver of health is a wasted zap.
glossary.example: At TH9, one plan uses six Lightning Spells and one Earthquake Spell to zap two Air Defenses.

glossary.short: Lava Hounds and Balloons together. Also written Lalo or LavaLoon.
means: The name joins Lava Hound and Balloon. The Lava Hounds go first and tie up the Air Defenses, then the Balloons follow and destroy defences while the Air Defenses are busy.

It is a classic air attack, but it depends on timing. Balloons sent too soon arrive before the Hounds have taken the fire, and sent too late they arrive after the Hounds have died. Zap Lalo removes an Air Defense with Lightning first.
glossary.example: Send Lava Hounds first, then Balloons close behind with Haste and Healing Spells.

glossary.short: An air army mixing Dragon Riders with other big flyers, often hitting from two sides.
means: Hydra is used loosely. At its simplest it means Dragon Riders with Dragons or Electro Dragons, so you are not relying on one troop. Many guides also describe it as a two-flank air attack, which makes Air Defenses split their fire.

Our armies called Hydra all mix several air troops, usually with Balloons or a Lava Hound, but differ otherwise. Super Archer Clone Hydra opens with a Battle Blimp, and Dragon Duke Charge Hydra opens with the Duke.
Routes decide it, so plan around the Air Defenses and Clan Castle. It suits Air Defenses you can split, and fails when they sit central under Wizard Towers.
glossary.example: Open with a Lava Hound and Balloons on one flank, then send Dragons and Dragon Riders with Rage and Freeze.

glossary.short: A Golem and Hog Rider attack, with Wizards in our version.
means: Go stands for Golems and Ho for Hog Riders. Golems take the fire on one side while Wizards clear a funnel, and then Hog Riders run through the gap to go after defences.
It teaches timing and spell placement, because Hog Riders die quickly if they meet Giant Bombs or splash without healing. Older guides warn that it needs careful scouting.
glossary.example: Heal the Hog Riders at the spot where defences overlap, rather than where they stand now.

glossary.short: Golems in front, Witches behind, winning by steady pressure.
means: Witches keep raising Skeletons, which distract defences and soak up shots. In our plan, Golems lead and Witches follow through a gap made by Wall Breakers or a Jump Spell. It does not take precise timing.
Guides differ on the details. Some put Witches on two corners first, with Healers, to make a funnel, and then send a Golem and heroes into the core. Army names like this are often used loosely.
glossary.example: Golems first to take the fire, then Witches behind them, then Rage, Freeze and Healing as needed.

glossary.short: The Archer Queen and a group of Healers moving around the base together.
means: Healers follow the Archer Queen and heal the damage she takes. With four or five of them she can go on removing buildings for a long time.
Her usual job is clearing the edge of a base to set up a funnel, or removing one chosen target. Air Defenses are the danger, because when they kill the Healers she falls quickly.
glossary.example: Walk the Queen down one side with her Healers, keeping clear of Air Defenses, then send the main army.

glossary.short: The Archer Queen with Healers, sent to clear a whole side before the army follows.
means: It uses the same pair as a Queen Walk, but gives her a bigger job. Drop four to six Healers together, a beat after the Queen. She then removes several key defences and clears one side, often after Wall Breakers have got her into a compartment.

Our Queen Charge plans follow with a Hybrid of Hog Riders and Miners. Other follow-ups are possible, such as LaLoon. Some guides, and at times ours, use Queen Walk and Queen Charge for the same thing. QC is the short form.
glossary.example: Walk the Queen with Healers on one side, keeping her away from single target Inferno Towers, then send Hog Riders and Miners.

glossary.short: RC means Royal Champion. Here she clears a route while spells keep her alive.
means: RC is short for Royal Champion. She has short range and goes for defences, jumping walls to do so. Start from a corner where she can move inward. Cast Invisibility about every 10 seconds, so she keeps removing defences and leaves a funnel behind her.

When the walk is finished, your Dragons or Root Riders follow along the side she cleared. You can recall her once the Invisibility runs out. It takes precise control, because a badly placed spell loses her.
glossary.example: Walk the Royal Champion with Invisibility, then send Root Riders with Overgrowth along the cleared side.

glossary.short: The Royal Champion sent in to strip key defences as part of the main attack.
means: In an RC Charge she goes after particular defences, such as a Spell Tower or those around the Town Hall. Electro Boots and Invisibility are common choices for keeping her alive.
She goes before the main group, with a tank taking the first hits. Guides overlap with RC Walk, so treat the name as a rough guide and read the steps.
glossary.example: Charge the Royal Champion along one side, then send Root Riders through the defences she has weakened.

glossary.short: The Dragon Duke sent in first to clear a side, with an air army following.
means: The Dragon Duke is a tough flying hero who gets stronger when no friendly flyers are near him. A Duke Charge uses that. He goes in alone, supported by spells such as Invisibility, Revive or Totem, and clears what he can before the rest fly in.

Keep your other flyers well away from him, or they switch off the bonus. Scout for Seeking Air Mines, as recent changes make traps hurt him more. Our plan follows with Inferno Dragons, a Lava Hound, Rocket Balloons and Dragon Riders.
Ground-led armies may send him after the ground group instead.
glossary.example: Charge the Dragon Duke along one side using Invisibility, then send your air troops on a different lane.

glossary.short: The Grand Warden and Healers moving round the base to clear a side.
means: The Grand Warden has long range and little health, so Healers keep him going while he shoots. Healers cannot heal air units, so use ground mode. Furnaces can help him make the funnel before the main group arrives.
It works like a Queen Walk, though you also have his ability and his Fireball, if he wears it, to think about. Keep the ability back for the moment it is most needed.
glossary.example: Open with the Warden and Healers on one side, then fire his Fireball at a stack of defences.

glossary.short: The Grand Warden leads with Healers, and the main army pushes in behind him.
means: Our Warden Charge Super Yetis plan opens with the Warden and Healers, uses Furnaces and Skeleton Spells to pull fire, and then sends Super Yetis behind him, with Jump where walls block them.
It is loosely named. Some guides call the opening of this same army a Warden walk, so the two names can mean the same thing.
glossary.example: Warden and Healers first, then Super Yetis behind, with a Jump Spell on the blocking wall.

glossary.short: A heavy ground attack led by Root Riders, which break walls very quickly.
means: Root Riders are tough ground troops that smash walls and go for defences, so walls hold them up far less than most ground troops. A group of them goes through a walled base with Overgrowth and Rage helping. It is often rated the most consistent ground army at high Town Halls.

Our Root Rider Yeti is one form of it. Root Riders push the defences and Super Yetis follow into the core, with a hero charge alongside. Its weak point is the Monolith, which hits high health troops hardest.
glossary.example: The King and Giants make the funnel, then Root Riders go in, followed by Super Yetis into the core.

glossary.short: Yetis sent behind a tank to overwhelm the base on the ground.
means: Yetis hit hard, and they release small Yetimites as they take damage, which add to the pressure. Sent through a funnel behind a tank such as an Ice Golem, they flood the core.
It is a ground alternative to Dragons from about TH12. Multi-target Inferno Towers are its main problem, as they cut through a swarm.
glossary.example: Make a funnel with heroes, send Yetis behind an Ice Golem, then Rage and Freeze as they reach the core.

glossary.short: Dragons followed by a swarm from Bat Spells.
means: The name joins Dragons and Bats. Dragons go first and deal with what would kill Bats quickly, such as Wizard Towers and other splash defences. Bat Spells then flood the part of the base that is left.
Bats die quickly to splash, so timing decides the attack. Older guides split it differently, with Dragons on the side away from the Air Defenses and Bats taking those Air Defenses.
glossary.example: Deploy Dragons with a Battle Blimp, wait until the splash defences are gone, then drop Bat Spells on what is left.

glossary.short: Short for suicide. Heroes dive early to remove defences, without being expected to survive.
means: In a sui, heroes and a few tanks go deep early on to remove key defences. They may well not come back, and that is fine if they took out enough. Players talk about the value of a sui, meaning what it removed.
It is usually the first half of an attack. The classic form is Sui Lalo, where Lava Hounds and Balloons follow through the space it opened.
glossary.example: Sui Lalo at TH12: a Golem and Ice Golem tank for the heroes, then Lava Hounds and Balloons finish the base.

glossary.short: Golems, Wizards and P.E.K.K.As attacking on the ground together.
means: Go stands for Golems, Wi for Wizards and Pe for P.E.K.K.As. Golems take the fire, Wizards clear the way, and P.E.K.K.As hit what is left.
It is an older army, mostly heard of at the lower Town Halls. Our plans do not use it, but you will still see the name.

glossary.short: Grand Warden equipment that throws an explosion at the closest defence. Armies are named after it.
means: Fireball is epic hero equipment for the Grand Warden. When fired, it throws a big exploding ball at the closest defence, which can flatten a group of defences that sit close together. Fireball Super Yeti opens the base this way and then sends Super Yetis through the hole.

It needs a high level to work well, at about level 24. Below that, it may leave a damaged defence standing and not the empty space you planned for, so bring Earthquake to finish it. Aim is set by where the Warden stands, so walk him to the right spot first. Many plans use Invisibility to lock the target.
glossary.example: Soften defences with the Warden's Fireball, then send Super Yetis with the King and Royal Champion.

glossary.short: Dragon Duke equipment that flies him in a straight line across the base.
means: When fired, the Dragon Duke flies across the base in a straight line, breathing fire. While flying he cannot be targeted, traps do not go off, and the Clan Castle stays inactive.

He always flies through the centre, so where you drop him sets the line. A little off is a big miss. Let him reach the first defences before firing. He lands exposed on the far side, so have follow-up ready, or a Recall Spell. Rocket Backpack Throwers opens with this flight, then sends Throwers and Healers.
glossary.example: Open with the Dragon Duke on Rocket Backpack, then open walls with Wall Breakers and send Throwers and Healers.

glossary.short: A building that holds troops donated by your clan. Also called the CC.
means: Your clan mates can send you troops, spells and Siege Machines, which sit in your Clan Castle. When you attack, you can drop those troops like any others. A Siege Machine can carry them into the base for you.

On defence, the enemy's castle does the same in reverse. Its troops come out when an attacker gets close, and can stop a hero or a push by surprise. So guides often say to lure them out first, or to plan your path around the castle.
glossary.example: Clan Castle troops can be sent in a Battle Blimp to land next to a key defence.

glossary.short: The main building of a base. TH followed by a number gives its level, as in TH13.
means: Your Town Hall level decides what you can build and which troops, spells and heroes are open to you. Advice is often given by level because the same army can be strong at TH9 and useless at TH14.
It also matters in an attack. Destroying the enemy's Town Hall earns a star on its own. From TH12 to TH17 it fights back with a weapon, and at TH18 a Guardian defends it instead.
At TH18 it no longer counts as a defence, so troops that target defences skip it. Plan who destroys it.
glossary.example: Root Riders open at TH15, so a Root Rider plan is no use to a TH14 player.

glossary.short: How much room a troop or spell takes up in your army.
means: Your army has a limited amount of room, and each troop takes a set share of it. A Barbarian takes 1, a Dragon 20, a Golem 30. A strong troop costs more than a weak one, so every army is a trade-off.

Spells use their own separate space, and the same word applies. A Haste Spell takes one space and a Revive Spell two. Some effects also depend on it, such as the Eagle Artillery, which waits until 200 housing has been deployed.
glossary.example: A Yeti takes 18 housing and a Super Yeti takes 35, so boosting it changes how many you can bring.

glossary.short: Damage that hits everything in an area, not just one target.
means: Splash hits the target and whatever stands near it. Mortars, Wizard Towers and Bomb Towers use it against your troops, so a tight clump of weak troops can vanish in one shot. That is why guides say to spread them out.
It works for you too. Wizards, Baby Dragons and Super Bowlers hit several buildings at once, which suits a packed core. A defence's splash radius tells you how far it reaches.
glossary.example: One Mortar shell can kill a clump of Archers, so drop them in a line.

glossary.short: Hits only one thing at a time.
means: A single target defence or troop puts all its damage on one target and moves on only when that target is gone. It is deadly against a hero or tank, but slow against many small units.

So you beat single target defences with numbers or distractions. Skeletons and swarms waste their shots. Inferno Towers are the main example, because a single target Inferno builds up the longer it stays on one target.
glossary.example: Keep your Queen clear of single target Inferno Towers, or Freeze them as they lock on.

glossary.short: Hits several separate targets at the same moment.
means: A multi-target defence fires at several enemies at once, with less damage on each than a single target one. It is at its best against swarms of small troops and weak against one big tank.
An Inferno Tower can be set by its owner to single or multi-target, so check which it is when you scout. A Multi-Archer Tower hits three targets at once.
glossary.example: Multi-target Inferno Towers cut through a swarm of Yetis and Yetimites.

glossary.short: An attack that jumps from one target to others close by.
means: A chain attack hits one target and then leaps to the next one in reach, usually for less damage each time. Spacing decides how well it does. Close buildings or close troops take more hits, and spread ones break the chain.

It works in both directions. Electro Dragons and Super Wizards chain through your enemy's buildings. A Super Wizard Tower chains through your troops, up to 15 targets, and a Ricochet Cannon's shot bounces on to a second target.
glossary.example: Send Electro Dragons in a straight line through buildings that sit close together.

glossary.short: An area around a unit that affects everything nearby.
means: An aura goes with the unit and affects things inside its range. Some help your troops, as with the Apprentice Warden, whose aura gives nearby troops extra health. Others hurt the enemy, as with the Electro Titan, whose aura damages everything around her.
To get the most from a helping aura, drop it where the most friends will stand inside it, usually mid-group and not at the front.
glossary.example: Walk an Apprentice Warden with tough troops, since his aura only reaches 7 tiles.

glossary.short: Melee means hitting at arm's length. Ranged means shooting from further off.
means: A melee unit has to walk right up to its target, so walls and other troops can hold it up, and it takes the fire when it gets there. A ranged unit shoots from a distance, often over walls, and usually has less health.
Reach is why some pets and heroes fit badly together. A pet with short range may run far ahead of a hero who attacks from long range.
glossary.example: Valkyries are melee and need a way through walls, while Archers can shoot over them.

glossary.short: One square of the grid a base is built on, used to measure distance.
means: A base sits on a grid. Each square is a tile. Building sizes such as 3x3 count tiles, and so do ranges and spell sizes.
It helps you place things. Knowing a Healing Spell reaches 5 tiles or a defence shoots 9 tiles tells you where to drop things and who is safe.
glossary.example: Place a Healing Spell 3 to 4 tiles ahead of the group, so they walk into it.

glossary.short: A distance too close for a defence to hit. Also called a blind spot.
means: Some defences cannot shoot anything right next to them. Troops that get inside that distance are safe from that defence and can hit it freely.

The Eagle Artillery cannot hit closer than 7 tiles and the Scattershot closer than 3. The Mortar has a small gap as well. It explains why these defences are hard to deal with from far off, yet simple once your troops are next to them.
glossary.example: Once your troops reach an Eagle Artillery they no longer take its shots, though other defences still hit them.

glossary.short: Small units made by another troop, spell or pet during an attack.
means: You do not train these. They appear during the attack. Skeletons from a Witch are the simplest example. Yetimites come out of Yetis and Super Yetis as they take damage. Golemites and Lava Pups appear when a Golem or Lava Hound falls. Ice Pups do the same for an Ice Hound. Meteormites are the halves a Meteor Golem splits into.

Firemites come from a Furnace. A Super Witch summons a single Big Boy. A Ruin Witch turns rubble, which destroyed buildings leave behind, into Ruin Knights. Frostmites and Boogers come from the pets Frosty and Sneezy.
They can be a real part of your damage, and they keep drawing fire after their parent has gone. Some spells treat them differently. Ice Block misses any that appear after it lands.
glossary.example: Golemites keep drawing fire after a Golem falls, which gives your main troops extra time.

glossary.short: A built-in power-up some troops get when they are alone or angry. Not the Rage Spell.
means: Baby Dragons and the Dragon Duke become enraged when no other friendly flyers are near. They gain extra damage and attack speed while it lasts.
So these units want space. Sending other flyers alongside them, or giving the Duke a pet like Sneezy whose Boogers fly near him, can turn the bonus off.
glossary.example: Use one or two Baby Dragons away from your air group, so each one stays enraged while clearing the outside.

glossary.short: The best result an attack can get: all three stars. Also called a triple.
means: An attack can earn three stars. You get one for destroying 50% of the base, one for destroying the Town Hall, and one for destroying everything. A three-star therefore means the whole base went down.

To three-star a base, or an army's three-star rate, is the usual way players judge how good an attack is. A triple and tripling a base mean the same thing. A hit rate is the same idea: the share of attacks with an army that got all three.
glossary.example: Mass Dragons is often called the safest three-star at TH7.

glossary.short: A clan against clan contest, decided by total stars.
means: Two clans are matched and face off. After a preparation day comes a battle day, when each member can usually attack twice, and the clan with more stars wins.
Only the best attack on each base counts, so a repeat hit only adds new stars. If stars are level, total destruction decides.
Unlike a regular Battle, you can study the target base for as long as you like, and you get only two attacks. So guides favour armies that are reliable, and much advice here is aimed at war.
glossary.example: Greedy Raven is a farming pet, so swap it out before war unless your plan needs its storage damage.

glossary.short: Clan War League: a monthly event where clans play a series of wars.
means: Clan War League runs for part of each month. Your clan plays seven wars against the other clans in its group, and each member gets one attack per war. Results earn League Medals to spend in a special shop.
With one attack per war, there is no second try, so players look for safe armies. If a guide calls something good for CWL, it usually means dependable.
The Titan and Legend leagues also use Battle Modifiers, so expect harder attacks there.
glossary.example: In CWL, bring the army you have practised, as you only get one go in each war.

glossary.short: A stronger version of a normal troop that you pay to unlock for a few days.
means: From TH11, you can boost a troop you have levelled high enough into its super version. A boost costs 25,000 Dark Elixir and lasts three days. Super Yeti, Super Archer and Rocket Balloon are examples.
Each takes more housing than the normal troop, and most have a special ability of their own. As a boost is costly and time limited, check your plan before you pay.
glossary.example: Boosting Yetis into Super Yetis takes each one from 18 housing to 35.

glossary.short: A vehicle that carries your Clan Castle troops into the base. Built in the Workshop.
means: You build these in the Workshop from TH12 on. Most go somewhere useful, such as to the Town Hall, and release your Clan Castle troops when they finish or are destroyed. Some do the job in a different way, like a Log Launcher that clears walls ahead of it.
Spells mostly do not help them. A Healer will not heal one, and many lose health over time. Clan mates can also donate them to your Clan Castle.
glossary.example: A Wall Wrecker drives at the Town Hall, smashing walls on the way, then releases your Clan Castle troops.

glossary.short: A power you fire by tapping a hero's icon during an attack.
means: Heroes can do things beyond their normal attack. You tap the hero's icon once, and what happens depends on the equipment they wear, such as a burst of healing, a big strike or a shield for the army. You usually get one use in an attack.

Timing is often the difference between a hero surviving or not. Fire it too early and it is gone when the big hit comes. Fire it too late and the hero has already fallen. Some troops have named abilities of their own, which work without you doing anything.
glossary.example: Save the Warden's ability until the push is under heavy fire, not the moment you can use it.

glossary.short: Items a hero wears that change what they can do, upgraded with ore.
means: Each hero wears two pieces at a time, chosen from a set made for that hero. The Blacksmith opens at TH8, and upgrades now sit in the Hero Equipment tab of the Build menu. Shiny Ore is the most common, Glowy Ore is rarer, and Starry Ore is the rarest and only goes on epic pieces.

Common pieces come free as you upgrade the Blacksmith and reach level 18. Epic pieces come from events, the Trader or the Hero Journey, which is free, and reach level 27. Rarity does not always mean stronger, so check what your plan needs.
glossary.example: Spiky Ball is the usual first pick for the King. Earthquake Boots suit pushes that need walls broken.

glossary.short: Grand Warden equipment that makes him and nearby troops immune to damage for a moment.
means: When fired, the Grand Warden and friendly units close to him take no damage for a short time. It is the safest first upgrade for him, since it helps in almost any army.

Use it for the worst moment of the attack, such as when a group walks into a nest of defences. Troops that walk into his aura after you fire it are covered too, and cover lasts a second after they leave. Fire it the moment it is ready and you have nothing left for that. It is a piece of equipment, so a Warden not wearing it does not have it. An Apprentice Warden never does.
glossary.example: Save the Tome until your Yetis reach the core, then fire it as the Inferno Towers and bombs start hitting.

glossary.short: The two ways a Grand Warden can move, on foot or flying.
means: You choose before you deploy him. In ground mode he walks with ground troops and can walk over walls. In air mode he flies with an air army, and air-hitting defences can target him instead of ground ones.
Choose by the army he has to stay with, since his support only reaches nearby troops. Some pets suit one mode better. Boogers from Sneezy, for example, are said to work in air mode only.
An X-Bow has modes too, though for a different reason. Its owner sets it to ground only at long range, or to air and ground at a shorter range.
glossary.example: Walk him on foot with Super Yetis, and fly him with Dragons.

glossary.short: Extra upgrade stages for a building already at its final level.
means: When a building is fully upgraded at the top Town Hall, you can spend a builder and resources on small extra boosts. A defence usually gets two stages, each adding a bit of damage or health. They are cheaper and smaller than a normal upgrade.

They do not last forever. When Supercell releases a new level for that building, its supercharges reset. For an attacker, it means a top level defence can be a little stronger than its level suggests.

glossary.short: Two defences at high levels combined into one stronger building.
means: From TH16, you can merge two maxed defences to make a new one. Two Archer Towers at level 21 become a Multi-Archer Tower, and two Cannons at level 21 become a Ricochet Cannon.

A Multi-Gear Tower at TH17 takes a geared up Archer Tower and a geared up Cannon. At TH18, two level 17 Wizard Towers become a Super Wizard Tower. Each has an attack the originals lacked, so old advice about those buildings no longer fits.
glossary.example: A Ricochet Cannon's shot bounces on to a second target, so a line of troops is not as safe as it once was.

glossary.short: A Builder Base upgrade that gives a home defence a second way of firing.
means: A Cannon, an Archer Tower and a Mortar can each be geared up once you have their partner building on the Builder Base. The Master Builder does the work, and it costs home village Gold. You need the defence at the listed level too.

A geared up defence gets a new mode. A Cannon or Mortar gets Burst mode, and an Archer Tower gets Fast attack mode. It shoots much faster, though Cannons and Archer Towers lose some range for it. A geared up pair can also feed the Multi-Gear Tower later on.
glossary.example: A geared up Cannon in Burst mode reaches less far, but fires far faster.

glossary.short: A defending unit that protects the Town Hall at TH18. Attackers cannot use them.
means: At TH18, the Town Hall lost its own weapon and gained a Guardian. The defender picks one: the Smasher, the Longshot or the Logger. It stands on the Town Hall, then jumps down and fights once enemies come within range.

The Smasher is melee, and it hits with splash. It rages when the Town Hall falls, and leaves Rage behind when it is defeated. The Longshot is ranged with splash and explodes when defeated. The Logger rolls slow logs through everything in their path and knocks targets back.
All of them hit both ground and air. Poison works on them at reduced damage. A Frozen Guardian does not wake, so a Freeze can hold it on the Town Hall while your troops get close.
With no weapon, the TH18 Town Hall no longer counts as a defence. Troops that target defences, such as Hog Riders and Balloons, walk past it. It still earns the star, so plan who destroys it.
Each Guardian has its own page under Defences and traps.
glossary.example: Check which Guardian is on the Town Hall, and keep a Freeze for when you reach it.

glossary.short: The spells a Spell Tower can cast on the defending side.
means: A Spell Tower casts one spell to help the defence, chosen by the defender. Rage comes at level 1, Poison at 2, Invisibility at 3 and Earthquake at 4.

Rage makes defences hit harder. Poison hurts and slows your troops. Invisibility hides defences for a moment. Earthquake takes a share of ground troops' health. After casting, it needs time to recharge, so it can fire again in a long attack.
Bait a cast first, destroy the tower, or Freeze it before it casts. A destroyed tower casts nothing, but a Freeze will not stop a spell already running.
glossary.example: Rage from a Spell Tower makes nearby defences hit much harder, so Freeze the tower before it casts, not after.

glossary.short: An Inferno Tower runs in one of two modes. Single-target melts big troops, multi-target hits swarms.
means: In single-target mode, the beam stays on one unit and grows stronger the longer it holds. It melts heroes and tanks, but a swarm wastes its time.
In multi-target mode, it hits several units at once for low, steady damage. It cuts through swarms and small troops, but healing and big tanks can outlast it.
The owner picks the mode, so check each Inferno when you scout. The tower looks different in each.
Freeze, Invisibility and Ice Block are the usual answers to the single-target beam. Breaking its lock with Invisibility resets it, so it has to build up again.
glossary.example: Cast Invisibility on a hero as an Inferno starts to burn, and the beam has to start over.
Try a new army in regular Battles first, then bring it to Ranked once you trust it.
glossary.short: The attack mode where trophies move. It opens at TH7, with a limited number of attacks.
means: Since October 2025, online attacks come in two modes. Trophies are only won or lost in Ranked Battles. Regular Battles risk none.
Ranked runs as Tournaments, most of them weekly. You face players in your Town Hall range, and your results move you up or down a League. Trophies reset after each Tournament.
Attacks and defences are both limited, so each one counts. Pick an army you trust. Ranked pays some loot, but regular Battles are the place to raid.
Temporary troops and spells from events are not allowed here, or in war and CWL.

glossary.example: Test a new army in regular Battles, where a failed attack costs you no trophies.
glossary.short: The everyday attack mode, open from TH2. Attacks are unlimited, with no trophies at risk.
means: Regular Battles match you mostly by Town Hall level. You can attack as often as you like and cannot lose trophies, so this is the place to raid and to practise.
Your base can still be raided here. After an attack on it you get a Magic Shield for a while, and attacking does not cut that short.

glossary.example: A strong week in Ranked moves you up a League, where the attacks get harder and the bonuses grow.
glossary.short: Your tier in Ranked Battles. Your results move you up or down.
means: Ranked players are sorted into named tiers such as Titan, Dragon and Electro, with Legend at the top. At the end of a Tournament, the best in your group promote and the weakest demote.
Each Town Hall has a floor, the lowest League it can sit in while you stay active. If you stop playing Ranked for some weeks, you slowly drop towards it.
Your League helps set your League Bonus and Star Bonus, which you earn in regular Battles as well as Ranked. So climbing pays off beyond trophies.
Legend League has three tiers, and all three use Battle Modifiers. CWL has its own separate ladder of leagues.

glossary.example: A hero charge that works in your usual wars may fall short in Legend, as the hero has less health and damage there.
glossary.short: Extra rules in the top leagues that make attacks harder.
means: Battle Modifiers make defences and defending heroes stronger, and attacking heroes weaker. Guardians get stronger too. In Ranked they apply in the three Legend tiers. In CWL they apply in the Titan and Legend leagues.
The higher the league, the harder they bite. Supercell has changed the amounts several times, so this guide gives none.
An army's usual three-star rate will not carry over, and plans that lean on a hero feel it most. Tournament Mode in a friendly challenge is a good way to practise for them.

glossary.example: The Inferno Artillery is always active, so it fires from the moment your attack starts.
glossary.short: A weapon built into the Town Hall from TH12 to TH17. TH18 has none.
means: From TH12 the Town Hall fights back. TH12 has the Giga Tesla, TH13 to TH16 have the Giga Inferno, and TH17 has the Inferno Artillery. At TH12 to TH16 it also goes off as a death bomb when destroyed.
The TH12 to TH16 weapons have no levels of their own, so they are always at full strength.
Building the Inferno Artillery uses up the Eagle Artillery, so TH17 and TH18 bases have no Eagle.
A weapon is part of the building and goes when the Town Hall falls. A Guardian is a separate unit that moves, fights and has to be dealt with on its own.
Each weapon has its own page under Defences and traps.

glossary.short: A temporary defence the owner picks and upgrades at the Crafting Station.
means: The choice changes each crafting season, and old ones are removed when a season ends. So you may meet one you have not seen, and scouting matters more.

They used to appear only at the top Town Halls. The set from August 2026 opens at TH11. Hero Hunter goes after heroes, Hot Candle burns out as the attack goes on, and Cake-A-Pult leaves delayed bombs.

glossary.example: Healer Puppet brings a flock of Healers to keep the Archer Queen alive.
glossary.short: Hero equipment that summons small troops to fight beside the hero.
means: You fire it with the hero's ability, and the summoned troops appear around the hero. They add damage or healing, and they give defences something else to shoot.

glossary.short: Short for Hog Riders.
means: Hog Riders jump walls and go straight for defences, so they are fast but easily wiped by traps and splash. Players nearly always call them Hogs.
A Super Hog Rider is a separate boosted troop, so check which one a plan means.
glossary.example: Heal the Hogs where defences overlap.

glossary.short: The Gold, Elixir and Dark Elixir you take from a base you attack.
means: Attacking lets you steal part of what another player holds in their storages and collectors. Destroying those buildings gets you the loot inside.
Loot pays for your upgrades. Regular Battles are unlimited and risk no trophies, so they are the place to raid. Ranked Battles pay some loot too, but their attacks are limited.
You get less for hitting a lower Town Hall, and a bonus for hitting a higher one. A troop or pet that is good for loot goes for those resource buildings, and may not help you win a war.
glossary.example: Goblins run for storages first, so they suit raids for loot but not war.

glossary.short: Attacking mainly to collect resources rather than to win stars.
means: Upgrades are costly, so players spend a lot of attacks raiding for Gold and Elixir in regular Battles. Armies cost nothing to train and are ready at once, so you can raid as often as you like.
A farming army goes for storages and does not need three stars.

Players look for dead bases, meaning inactive villages whose collectors have filled up. They are full of easy loot, since nobody has been around to collect it. A raid in our guide means this kind of attack.
glossary.example: A Greedy Raven does extra damage to resource buildings, which is why it is a farming pet.

glossary.short: To study a base before you attack it.
means: Before you attack, you look over the base. Note where Air Defenses and Inferno Towers sit, whether each Inferno is single or multi-target, and where traps might be hiding in gaps.
In war you get as long as you like, so take at least 30 seconds. A plan that does not fit the base often fails however well you carry it out.
glossary.example: Check where the Clan Castle reaches, so you know whether your hero will wake its troops.

glossary.short: A free practice attack on a clan mate's base.
means: You can post a challenge in clan chat, and a clan mate can attack your base. Nothing is lost, and no trophies or loot change hands. Heroes and pets work even while upgrading.

It is the safest place to try an army or a new unit before risking a war attack. Tick Tournament Mode for a tougher test, with stronger defences and weaker heroes. Guides are thin on some newer units, so testing here may tell you more.
glossary.example: Try a new army in a friendly challenge before using it in war.

glossary.short: A change by Supercell that makes something stronger.
means: Supercell adjusts troops and defences through balance updates. When something gets stronger, it has been buffed. A buff can make old advice about it out of date.
So a guide written before a buff can undersell what it describes.
glossary.example: Hog Riders had a health buff in October, so older low ratings may no longer be fair.

glossary.short: A change by Supercell that makes something weaker.
means: The opposite of a buff. When a unit is too strong, Supercell cuts its health, damage or something else, and players say it was nerfed.
Figures gathered before a nerf can flatter what they describe, as our guide warns in a few places.
glossary.example: Fire Heart was nerfed in October, so older figures for Dragon Duke armies may overstate them.

glossary.short: Whichever armies and tactics are most popular and effective right now.
means: The meta is what most strong players are using at the moment. It shifts as Supercell changes the game and players find new ideas.
It is a helpful starting point, not a rule. An army can be strong and out of the meta, particularly at lower Town Halls, where the top players' choices matter less.

glossary.example: Send the Loons behind a Lava Hound, so it takes the Air Defense fire.
glossary.short: Short for Balloons.
means: Players often call Balloons Loons, and Rocket Balloons Rocket Loons. LaLoon gets its name the same way.

glossary.example: Mass Drags means an army that is nearly all Dragons.
glossary.short: Short for Dragons. E-Drags are Electro Dragons.
means: Players shorten most Dragons to Drags, as in Mass Drags, E-Drags, Baby Drags and Super Drags. Each is a different troop, so check which one a plan means.

glossary.example: Time your Balloons so they pass while the Pups are still taking shots.
glossary.short: Short for Lava Pups, the small flyers a Lava Hound releases when it dies.
means: They keep drawing fire for a moment after the Hound has gone. An Ice Hound has its own version, called Ice Pups.

glossary.example: Zap the AD means use Lightning to destroy an Air Defense.
glossary.short: What players call defences and heroes in clan chat.
means: For defences, AD is Air Defense, Xbow is X-Bow, Eagle is Eagle Artillery, Scatter is Scattershot, and Sweeper is Air Sweeper.
For heroes, BK is the Barbarian King, AQ the Archer Queen, GW the Grand Warden, RC the Royal Champion, and MP the Minion Prince.

glossary.example: Spend your spare Lightning on the expos, so your Balloons have fewer defences to pass.
glossary.short: A defence left exposed outside the walls, so it is easy to reach.
means: Expo is short for exposed. A defence sitting at the edge is cheap to remove with a hero, a few Lightning Spells or long range troops. Do that before the main army goes in.

glossary.example: Send your heroes at the defences that matter most, so they get value before they fall.
glossary.short: What a hero, spell or pet got done before it ended.
means: A hero that falls after removing three key defences got good value. One that falls at the first wall got none.
Players use the word to judge whether something was worth it, not whether it survived. That is why a sui can still be a success.

glossary.example: If a clan mate has already tripled your mirror, you may be asked to dip for the stars left elsewhere.
glossary.short: Hitting the enemy base at your own war rank, or a lower one.
means: The war map ranks each clan's bases from strongest to weakest. Your mirror is the enemy base at the same rank as yours.
To dip is to hit a lower base for a safer three-star. Clans often use it late in a war to pick up stars others have missed.

glossary.short: A base layout built to stop a three-star. An anti-two protects the second star.
means: An anti-three spreads its defences and traps so an attacker gets two stars but runs out of army before the last buildings fall.
An anti-two guards the Town Hall and the 50% mark, so even the second star is hard to get. Both are common in war, so scout for what the base wants you to do.

glossary.short: Rushed means the Town Hall went up before the rest. Maxed means everything is at its top level.
means: A rushed base has a high Town Hall with low defences for that level, so it is often easier than its Town Hall suggests.
A maxed base has every defence at the top level for its Town Hall, so expect the full challenge. The same words apply to an attacker's troops and heroes.

Barbarian Puppet.tip: Starter piece. Raged Barbarians add bodies and distraction, but swap it out once you own an Epic.

Rage Vial.tip: Rages him for more damage and speed. Strong early, then a cheap partner for Giant Gauntlet in compartment pushes.

Earthquake Boots.tip: Stomp breaks walls and softens buildings. Pick it to open compartments, or beside Spiky Ball, which finishes what it softens.

Vampstache.tip: A small heal on every hit. A stopgap only, as it cannot keep up with heavy defences at high Town Halls.

Giant Gauntlet.tip: Turns him into a splash tank who takes far less damage. Pick it when he must lead a push through a compartment.

Spiky Ball.tip: His most flexible piece and the usual first upgrade. It bounces between buildings, so it clears a corner or finishes softened targets.

Snake Bracelet.tip: Passive. Snakes appear as he takes damage and distract defences, so it suits a King who tanks for a long time.

Stick Horse.tip: Passive. He hops walls and fights faster for a while after landing. Pick it for a deep push, and place him with care.

Archer Puppet.tip: Starter piece. Hidden Archers can pull an Inferno off her early on, but they add little at high Town Halls.

Invisibility Vial.tip: Hides her and makes her shots hit hard. Pick it to reset a single-target Inferno, mostly below the top Town Halls.

Giant Arrow.tip: For air attacks. One arrow pierces the whole base with double damage to Air Defenses, and does less elsewhere since May 2026.

Healer Puppet.tip: Summons Healers, so a Queen Walk needs fewer from your camps. Best at lower Town Halls, often beside an arrow piece.

Frozen Arrow.tip: Passive. Her shots slow what they hit, defences included, which helps on a long walk. October 2026 raised the slow.

Magic Mirror.tip: Summons copies of her that add damage and draw fire. A top war pick, often beside Action Figure.

Action Figure.tip: Summons a Giant Giant to tank and hides her for a second. The Epic to level first for most Queen attacks.

Monolith Arrow.tip: Passive. Shots add a share of the target's health. The bonus shrinks as you deploy more, so send her early.

Eternal Tome.tip: Everyone in his ring takes no direct damage for a few seconds. The safest first upgrade. Save it for the core.

Life Gem.tip: Passive aura that adds health to nearby troops. Best with sturdy troops rather than small swarms, usually beside the Eternal Tome.

Rage Gem.tip: Passive aura that adds damage to nearby troops. Pick it for smash attacks, but do not count on it adding to a Rage Spell.

Healing Tome.tip: A healing field that moves with him. Pick it for slow ground pushes, usually beside the Eternal Tome.

Fireball.tip: Throws a big splash at the closest defence, so position him first. Pick it to crack a compartment, often beside the Tome.

Lavaloon Puppet.tip: Summons small Lavaloons that hunt Air Defenses. Only for air attacks, and rarely the best choice.

Heroic Torch.tip: Troops in his aura walk through walls, move faster and take less damage. Strong on the ground, but it can upset your pathing.

Royal Gem.tip: A large extra heal and little else. The weakest of her kit, so replace it when you can.

Seeking Shield.tip: Bounces between defences at any distance. Best for opening a funnel or picking off weak defences at the edge.

Hog Rider Puppet.tip: Summons Hogs to tank and hides her briefly. Good against swarms or when you own no Epics. Weak to Giant Bombs.

Haste Vial.tip: Sharply raises her speed and attack rate for a short time. The usual partner for Electro Boots on a fast charge.

Rocket Spear.tip: Her next few throws reach far and hit harder, aimed at the nearest defence. Pick it for targets deep in the base.

Electro Boots.tip: Passive. A lightning aura hits everything around her and clears Skeletons. Her first piece to level.

Frost Flake.tip: Freezes several of the nearest defences for a few seconds. Useful support for the army, but it adds no damage to her charge.

Fire Heart.tip: Passive. His main healing, as Healers cannot reach him. October 2026 removed its damage, so weigh it against his other pieces.

Flame Blower.tip: A cone of fire the way he faces. Pick it for burst in a compartment. Beside Rocket Backpack it fires first, so aim him.

Stun Blaster.tip: Stuns nearby defences and troops. Pick it for war, and fire it as an Inferno or Monolith comes into reach.

Electro Fangs.tip: Passive. His hits chain to targets nearby, which helps on packed bases and against swarms. Competes with Fire Heart for a slot.

Rocket Backpack.tip: Flies him through the base centre, untargetable, burning the line. He lands alone at the far side, so line up the angle.

Revenge Deck.tip: Passive. Throws a card back at whatever damages him and heals a little, so it pays most under steady fire.

Henchmen Puppet.tip: Two bodyguards that soak traps and fire, with a short spell of invisibility. A solid choice before you own an Epic.

Dark Orb.tip: A crystal drifts forward, slowing and hurting defences and troops it touches. Half of his usual pair, and his best Common.

Metal Pants.tip: Cuts the damage he takes for a while. Fire it as he nears likely Seeking Air Mines or a cluster of Air Defenses.

Noble Iron.tip: Passive. His first few shots reach farther and hit much harder, then the effect is spent. A low priority for most armies.

Dark Crown.tip: Passive. He gains health and damage in three steps as your troops fall, so it builds late. Half of his usual pair.

Meteor Staff.tip: Passive. Meteors keep striking the nearest defence at any range. Steady damage, and a good swap for the Crown in Dragon armies.

Portal Pendant.tip: Pulls him and nearby units back to redeploy, partly healed and faster, and saves him from a fatal hit. Niche, and poor with Dark Orb.

threats.name: Giga Tesla
threats.role: The TH12 Town Hall's own weapon. It hides until woken, then zaps several troops at once, air and ground.
use: It wakes when the Town Hall takes damage, or at 51% destruction. Walking near does not wake it.
One Earthquake wakes it when you choose, so Balloons, Giants and Hog Riders turn on to the Town Hall.
Freeze stops the zaps while your troops kill it.
It spreads its zaps over several troops, so one tank with a Healing Spell can stand under it for a while.
beware: Balloons, Giants and Hog Riders pass a sleeping Town Hall by, so wake it before they arrive.
The blast just after it falls. Freeze does not stop it, so keep your main army clear.
A sudden wake-up at 51%, with clean-up troops standing close to it.

threats.name: Giga Inferno
threats.role: The Town Hall's weapon from TH13 to TH16. It hides until woken, then burns several troops at once, air and ground.
use: It wakes when the Town Hall takes damage, or at 51% destruction. Walking near does not wake it.
One Earthquake wakes it when you choose, so Balloons, Giants and Hog Riders turn on to the Town Hall.
Freeze stops the beams while your troops kill it. It does not stop what happens when it falls.
It is built for groups, so one strong tank or hero copes far better than a crowd.

beware.t: The icy blast when it falls, which damages and slows nearby troops. Eternal Tome does not stop the slow.
The Poison it drops when it falls, which damages troops and slows them. Siege Machines are immune.

beware: Your main army standing beside it as it falls. Walk clear, or finish it with ranged troops from further back.

threats.name: Inferno Artillery
threats.role: The TH17 weapon, made by merging the Town Hall with the Eagle Artillery. Four seeking shots leave pools of fire.
use: Freeze it as your main push enters its range, which stops new shots.
Spread out and keep moving. Each pool burns any ground or air troop standing in it.
Its reach is far shorter than the Eagle's, so a funnel on the far side is often clear of it.
Nothing goes off when it falls, so troops can finish it from close up.
beware: It is active from the start of the attack. There is no housing count to wait for, as the Eagle had.
Giants, Balloons and Hog Riders treat this Town Hall as a defence, so they may turn on to it.
Few targets. With under four troops in range, the shots double up on the same ones.

threats.name: Town Hall 18
threats.role: It has no weapon and no longer counts as a defence. A Guardian on its roof fights for it instead.
use: Check which Guardian stands on the roof when you scout, as each changes your plan.
Plan who takes it. Send troops that hit any building, such as Valkyries or Dragons, along a path that reaches it.
It has no blast when it falls, but a living Smasher rages.
Stars count buildings, so you can earn them without killing the Guardian if your army survives it.
beware: Giants, Balloons, Hog Riders and other defence-targeting troops walk past it while any defence still stands.
Root Riders and the Royal Champion no longer head for it by themselves, so funnel them towards it.
A one-star ending. An army that only chases defences can pass 50% with the Town Hall still up.

threats.name: Smasher
threats.role: Melee Guardian and the toughest of the three. His splash hits ground and air, and he rages if the Town Hall falls.
use: He jumps down when troops come near. Freeze stops him, and holds him on the roof until it thaws.
Drop a Totem away from your army to pull his swings. He has to walk to every target.
Choose your order. Kill him first and the Town Hall falls quietly. Take the Town Hall first and he rages.
Poison does little to Guardians, so spend that spell space elsewhere.
beware: His death. He leaves Rage behind, so try to finish him away from your enemy's strongest defences.
Flyers are not safe from him. His swing reaches air troops as well as ground.
He moves fastest of the three, so he soon reaches a hurt hero.

threats.name: Longshot
threats.role: Ranged Guardian with the longest reach of the three. Her splash bolts hit ground or air, and she explodes when she dies.
use: She notices troops from further out than the others, so expect her early.
Freeze stops her, and holds her on the roof until it thaws. Save it for your main push.
Drop a Totem away from your army to draw her bolts off it.
Each bolt hits ground or air, never both, so a mixed army only loses one layer at a time.
beware: Her death blast. Keep key troops clear as she falls.
Tight packs of small troops, which her splash catches from range.
Poison does little to Guardians, so do not rely on it to slow her.

threats.name: Logger
threats.role: Ranged Guardian that rolls slow logs through everything in a line. The logs hit ground and air and push troops back.
use: He jumps down when troops come near. Freeze stops him and holds him on the roof. Poison does little.
Come from more than one side, so one log cannot roll through your whole army.
Drop a Totem off to one side, so his logs roll away from your main force.
He hits softest and fires slowest of the three, so the push is the bigger danger.
beware: Troops lined up behind a tank, as a log rolls on through everything in its path.
Healers behind a ground army. The push can split them from the troops they heal.
Unlike the other two, he has no listed death effect, so killing him is not a trap.

lines: Rebuild the Clan Castle first, so you can join a clan and start getting donated troops.
Build the Laboratory next and start on Archers, as research never ties up a builder.
Then the Barracks for Wall Breakers and more Army Camp space, as your Giants and Archers plan needs both.
Raise your storages after that, as they decide whether you can hold enough Gold for the next Town Hall.
Hero Hall first, as it puts the Barbarian King in every attack. He stays at level 1 until TH7.
Barracks next for Balloons, as your easy plan is built on them.
Laboratory after that, then research Balloons, which do most of the damage in that plan.
Then the Air Defense and Gold Storages, to stop Balloon raids and hold enough Gold for the next Town Hall.
Spell Factory first, as it opens the Lightning Spell your easy plan uses.
Laboratory next, then research Wizards and Lightning, the parts of your plan with new levels here.
Barracks for Wizards and the new Army Camp come next, so your push hits harder and holds more troops.
Then the Wizard Tower for splash against swarms, and Gold Storages so you can afford the next Town Hall.
Laboratory first, as Giants, Wizards and Wall Breakers all have new levels waiting behind it.
Spell Factory next for the Healing Spell, which keeps your ground push alive under fire.
Army Camps and Clan Castle follow, as they add troops to every attack you make.
Then the Air Sweeper to slow air attacks, and Gold Storages so you can afford the next Town Hall.
Laboratory first, then research Dragons, as research now starts to become your slowest queue.
Barracks for Dragons and Spell Factory for Rage come next, as your easy Mass Dragons plan needs both.
Build the Dark Elixir Drill and Storage early, as the King's upgrades open here and cost Dark Elixir.
Level the King when you stop attacking for a while, as an upgrading hero can't attack.
Hero Hall first, as it brings the Archer Queen and raises the King's level cap.
Laboratory next, then Dragons and Rage, as every part of your easy Mass Dragons plan has new levels here.
Build the second Dark Elixir Drill and the Blacksmith early, as two heroes share Dark Elixir and equipment needs ore.
Upgrade the Dark Barracks for Golems and Valkyries only if you are moving to a ground plan.
Laboratory and Hero Hall first. The Hall brings the Minion Prince and lifts every hero's level cap.
Place the Helper Hut early and hire the free Lab Assistant, as he speeds up your research.
Spell Factory for Jump and Freeze, then Dark Barracks for Witches, as your easy Witch Slap plan needs all three.
Queen first among heroes, as her levels pay off in the most attacks. Keep one builder on heroes.
Laboratory and Hero Hall first, as research and hero levels wait on them. Then keep the Queen upgrading.
Place the Inferno Towers straight away, as even at level 1 they change how attackers approach you.
Research Dragons, Lightning and Earthquake next, as your easy Zap Dragons plan relies on all three.
Then Army Camps and Clan Castle. More troops help every attack, and the Castle can now hold a donated siege machine.
Laboratory first, then Hero Hall for the Grand Warden, as your easy Zap Witches plan leans on him.
Level the Warden early. He upgrades with Elixir, so he doesn't compete with your Dark Elixir heroes.
Research Witches, Golems, Lightning and Earthquake next, as your easy plan relies on all four.
Build the Eagle Artillery first among defences, as it is the biggest defensive gain at this level.
Laboratory first, then research Dragons and Lightning, as your easy Zap Dragons plan needs them.
Workshop next, so you can train your own Battle Blimp instead of waiting on clan donations.
Keep the Queen and Warden upgrading, one at a time, as they carry the most attacks here.
Army Camps and Clan Castle next, as both help every attack. The Giga Tesla needs no upgrades now.
Laboratory first, then Workshop for the Log Launcher and research on Yetis, as your easy plan needs both.
Hero Hall next for the Royal Champion. Take her first levels straight away, as they finish quickly.
Then go back to the Queen and Warden, who carry the most attacks at this level.
Army Camps and Clan Castle help every attack, so do them before levelling your new Scattershots.
Laboratory and Pet House first. Each level opens a pet, and the Unicorn is the safest long-term pick.
Queen and Warden next, as your easy Super Dragons plan uses both. They come before pets for Dark Elixir.
Research Dragons and Balloons, as your Super Dragons take their level from Dragons.
Then Clan Castle and Builder's Huts. Upgraded huts shoot back, and Army Camps have no new level here.
Laboratory first, then Barracks for Root Riders, as the plan guides default to here is built on them.
Hero Hall next for the Dragon Duke. Take his quick early levels, but keep the Queen, Warden and Royal Champion ahead.
Pet House next, as four more pets open here. Put levels on your main hero's pet first.
Army Camps and Clan Castle help every attack, so do them before your new Spell Towers and Monolith.
Laboratory first, then research Yetis, as your easy Fireball Super Yeti plan takes its level from them.
Hero Hall next, then the Warden and Royal Champion, as your easy plan uses both. The Queen follows.
Spell Factory for the Totem Spell your plan uses, then Clan Castle. Army Camps have no new level here.
Merge your first Ricochet Cannon and Multi-Archer Tower early. They are your big new defences, and need maxed Cannons and Archer Towers.
Laboratory first, then research Yetis and Ice Golems, as your easy Fireball Super Yetis plan gains from both.
Hero Hall next, then the Queen and Warden, as two heroes near their cap beat levels spread evenly.
Army Camps and Clan Castle next, as both add troops to every attack from the day they finish.
Then the Inferno Artillery, Firespitters, Giga Bomb and new merges, as new defences give the biggest jump for builder time.
Laboratory first, then research Yetis, Rage and Freeze, as your easy Super Yeti plan gains from all three.
Hero Hall next, then the Queen and Warden, with the Royal Champion close behind as your plan charges her.
Army Camps and Clan Castle next. This Town Hall adds no new attack troops, so they are your easy gain.
Pick one Guardian and level it, as only one defends at a time. Then Super Wizard Towers and Revenge Tower.
